\chapter{Five Small Answers}
\label{ch:sa-small-answers}
\hlchaptermodality{49}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say then, as, only, again and again and oh in Sanskrit, and use any of the five on its own as a reply.}

Complete SA-C49-oh and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[tarhi]{\sk{तर्हि} (tarhi) — then, in that case}

\label{lesson:SA-C49-then}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{haṁsaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तर्हि}}
\textbf{\sk{तर्हि}} (\emph{tarhi}) — \textquotedblleft{}then, in that case\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{तर्हि}} — \textquotedblleft{}then, in that case\textquotedblright{}.

Said on its own it answers a condition. Somebody tells you how matters stand; \textbf{\sk{तर्हि}} is your \textquotedblleft{}then, all right\textquotedblright{}.

It is built on the same \emph{t-} that points for you in \sk{तत्} and in \sk{तत्र}. Those two point at a thing and at a place; \textbf{\sk{तर्हि}} points at a moment — at that time, and so, therefore.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A one-word answer to how things stand.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tarhi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{haṁsaḥ}, then \emph{tarhi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{तर्हि} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}then, in that case\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yathā]{\sk{यथा} (yathā) — as, in the way that}

\label{lesson:SA-C49-as}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{tarhi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{यथा}}
\textbf{\sk{यथा}} (\emph{yathā}) — \textquotedblleft{}as, in the way that\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{यथा}} — \textquotedblleft{}as, in the way that\textquotedblright{}.

You already say \sk{तथा}, \textquotedblleft{}so, in that way\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\sk{यथा}} is its partner, and the two travel together: \emph{yathā ... tathā}, \textquotedblleft{}as ... so\textquotedblright{}. Holding one of the pair, you now hold both.

Said back to somebody on its own, it works as \textquotedblleft{}just so, as you say\textquotedblright{} — an agreement rather than a description.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The other half of a pair you already had half of.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{yathā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tarhi}, then \emph{yathā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{यथा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}as, in the way that\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kevalam]{\sk{केवलम्} (kevalam) — only, merely}

\label{lesson:SA-C49-only}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{yathā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{केवलम्}}
\textbf{\sk{केवलम्}} (\emph{kevalam}) — \textquotedblleft{}only, merely\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{केवलम्}} — \textquotedblleft{}only, merely, nothing but\textquotedblright{}.

Put it in front of what you are naming and it narrows the claim: \textbf{\sk{केवलम्}} \sk{दुग्धम्}, \textquotedblleft{}only milk\textquotedblright{}. It is the ordinary Sanskrit \textquotedblleft{}only\textquotedblright{}, not a poetic one.

It also stands alone. Asked how much of a thing there is, \textbf{\sk{केवलम्}} on its own is a complete and slightly rueful answer.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word that narrows whatever it stands in front of.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kevalam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{yathā}, then \emph{kevalam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{केवलम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}only, merely\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[muhuḥ]{\sk{मुहुः} (muhuḥ) — again and again}

\label{lesson:SA-C49-again-and-again}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{kevalam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मुहुः}}
\textbf{\sk{मुहुः}} (\emph{muhuḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}again and again\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{मुहुः}} — \textquotedblleft{}again and again, over and over\textquotedblright{}.

You have \sk{पुनः} for \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}, meaning one more time. \textbf{\sk{मुहुः}} is the stronger one: not once more but repeatedly, and doubled as \emph{muhur muhuḥ} it is stronger still.

It belongs with \emph{muhūrta}, a short measured stretch of time. The picture underneath is a thing happening moment after moment after moment.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A stronger \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} than the one you had.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{muhuḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kevalam}, then \emph{muhuḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{मुहुः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}again and again\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aho]{\sk{अहो} (aho) — oh!}

\label{lesson:SA-C49-oh}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{kevalam} mean, and what did \emph{muhuḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अहो}}
\textbf{\sk{अहो}} (\emph{aho}) — \textquotedblleft{}oh!\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{अहो}} — \textquotedblleft{}oh!\textquotedblright{}.

It is the sound of being struck by something: delight, surprise or dismay, with the tone deciding which. \textbf{\sk{अहो}} on its own is a whole reply, and one of the few you can give without knowing what comes next.

It is two small cries stuck together rather than a word with parts, which is why there is no history to trace under it. Sanskrit wrote its exclamations down, and this one has been in the language for as long as anything in it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five more replies: then, as, only, again and again, and oh.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aho}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{tarhi} and \emph{aho} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{अहो} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}oh!\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
